findings.title: Dynamic imports run eagerly at module load, so nothing is lazy
findings.body: Every entry is `import("./app")`, evaluated when the `appStore` object literal is created. The first file that imports `@calcom/app-store` therefore starts loading all ~29 app packages, including their heavy SDKs and module-level side effects. This is the same eager loading as the old static imports, now with extra promise overhead and no code-splitting or cold-start benefit. Real lazy loading needs factories such as `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, called only when that app is needed.

findings.title: Eagerly created import promises can become unhandled rejections
findings.body: The promises are created at module load and only awaited much later, if at all. If any app module throws while loading (missing env, bad dependency), its promise rejects with no handler attached. Node's default unhandled-rejection behaviour then fires, which can crash the process or flood logs, even for requests that never use that app. Before, a failing app only broke code that touched it. With per-app lazy factories, the failure would surface only where the app is awaited.

findings.title: async forEach makes the surrounding try/catch ineffective
findings.body: The callback is now `async` because of `await getCalendar(...)`, and `forEach` neither awaits nor handles the returned promises. The `try { ... } catch` around it can no longer catch anything. A rejection from `getCalendar` (failed app import) or from `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled rejection instead of being logged. The function also continues to send emails and return `true` before the calendar and video deletions have finished. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try.

findings.title: async forEach makes the surrounding try/catch ineffective
findings.body: Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts. The `forEach(async ...)` callback is not awaited, so errors from `await getCalendar(...)`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` bypass the try/catch and surface as unhandled rejections. The reschedule flow then reports success and sends emails without waiting for the deletions. Await `Promise.all` over the references inside the try block.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget async forEach in requestReschedule can leave unhandled rejections and unfinished deletions
findings.body: The callback now awaits `getCalendar`, which loads an app module asynchronously, but `forEach` does not await it. There is no error handling around the calendar/video deletions. If the app import fails, or `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` rejects, the result is an unhandled rejection. The mutation also proceeds to send emails and webhooks and returns before the old calendar/video events are removed, which can be cut short in serverless environments. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`, ideally with per-item error handling.

findings.title: Recurring-cancel deletions are pushed into apiDeletes after it has already been awaited
findings.body: The `forEach(async ...)` now does `await getCalendar(credential)` and then `await deleteEvent(...)` before pushing into `apiDeletes`. `forEach` does not wait, so the pushes land after `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` has captured the array (and after the early `await apiDeletes` in the paid path). The calendar deletions for recurring bookings are therefore never awaited. The cancellation emails go out first, and a failure becomes an unhandled rejection. The extra async hop for the app import makes this race more likely. Build the promises with `map` and await them, or use a `for...of` loop as was done in the else branch.
